subtopic: Feedback loops and iteration
passage: The report was due at nine the next morning, and the cleaners' vacuum roared outside the glass door. Omkar's manager Pranav had left one line at the top of the file: "Not good enough." No example, no reason. Omkar read it four times. He messaged, "Which section?" and an hour later the reply came: "Overall." He felt stung, then stuck, with no idea where to begin. Near midnight he rewrote every page, changing charts and headings that may have been fine. In the morning Pranav skimmed the new version, said "Better," and went into a meeting. Omkar sat at his desk, no wiser about what had been wrong.

qa.q: What did Pranav write at the top of the report?
qa.a: Pranav wrote "Not good enough." with no example and no reason.

qa.q: What was Omkar feeling after reading the comment four times?
qa.a: Omkar felt stung and lost, because the comment hurt but gave him nothing to act on.

qa.q: What could Omkar ask Pranav to make the feedback usable?
qa.a: He could ask Pranav for one concrete spot that fell short and what better would look like there, ideally in a short talk instead of a message.

qa.q: How might Pranav see this review?
qa.a: Pranav may think a quick line is efficient when busy, without realising the comment left Omkar guessing and rewriting everything. 🤔

grounding: Shows a worker receiving a vague verdict with no example, feeling stung and lost and unable to act on it.

subtopic: Feedback loops and iteration
passage: Vishal, the senior editor, stopped at Payal's desk in the Bengaluru office with a printout of her brochure copy. "It's just not working. Make it sharper." "Which lines?" Payal asked. "Overall. You'll get it," he said, and took a call. She spent Tuesday swapping adjectives and rewrote the headline three times. On Wednesday he glanced at it in passing. "Still not it." Her eyes prickled. She said "Okay" brightly and walked to the pantry, where her tea had gone cold on the shelf. Back at her desk she opened a blank page and stared at it, more lost than on Monday.

qa.q: Where did Vishal stop with the printout?
qa.a: Vishal stopped at Payal's desk in the Bengaluru office.

qa.q: What was Payal feeling when she said "Okay" brightly on Wednesday?
qa.a: Payal was hurt and covering it, since her eyes prickled and she went to the pantry instead of showing it.

qa.q: What could Payal try to get useful feedback from Vishal?
qa.a: She could bring two versions and ask which line in each felt weakest and why, so the answer has to be specific.

qa.q: What would change for Payal if Vishal had pointed to one paragraph?
qa.a: She would know where to work and what to fix, and the comment would inform her instead of only stinging.

grounding: Shows a worker receiving vague comments with no example, feeling both stung and lost.

subtopic: Feedback loops and iteration

passage:
Dear Farhan,
Thank you for sending the deck this morning. The customer story on slide three is the strongest part: the delayed-parcel example made the problem clear to me in ten seconds. One thing to change: on slide seven the sales chart has no label on the vertical axis, and someone in the room will ask what the numbers mean before you can make your point. Could you add the label and one line saying what the chart shows? Then people will not lose the thread. I am free tomorrow at ten if you would like me to look again. You are close. 🙂
Kishore

qa.q: Which slide has the chart with no label on the vertical axis?
qa.a: Slide seven has the sales chart with no label on the vertical axis.

qa.q: What does Kishore want for Farhan by offering to look again tomorrow?
qa.a: Kishore wants Farhan to feel supported and able to act, and the closing line "You are close" shows encouragement instead of criticism.

qa.q: What could Farhan do first after reading the letter?
qa.a: Farhan could add a label to the vertical axis on slide seven and a one-line takeaway, then send the deck back to Kishore for a second look.

qa.q: How might Farhan feel reading this compared with a comment like "Not good enough"?
qa.a: Farhan would probably feel respected and clear about the next step, since one strong part and one exact spot with a reason leave little to defend.

grounding: Shows a reviewer naming what works, pointing to a concrete spot and giving the reason in a kind, timely note.

subtopic: Feedback loops and iteration
subtype: Giving feedback that can be used [Response]
passage: Same day, always. If I wait a week, the person has already made up a story about my silence. So when a junior sends me a report, I read it once for what works and say that first, honestly. This time it was the clean summary table. Then I pick one spot, page four, the paragraph with three numbers and no source, and I say why: a reader will doubt the rest if they cannot trace it. I suggest adding a source line. Then I stop. Sangeeta, you asked if it feels awkward. A bit. But when they come back with the fix and a question, I know it landed. Shankar

qa.q: Which page has the paragraph with three numbers and no source?
qa.a: Page four has the paragraph with three numbers and no source.

qa.q: How does Shankar feel about giving feedback, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Shankar feels a little awkward but sure of the approach, saying it feels awkward yet judging by the juniors who come back with the fix and a question that it lands.

qa.q: What makes Shankar's feedback something a junior can act on?
qa.a: It names what works first, points to one concrete paragraph, gives the reason and suggests a fix, all on the same day.

qa.q: What might the junior who sent the report feel if Shankar waited a week to reply?
qa.a: They might make up a story about the silence and expect the worst, which is why Shankar replies the same day.

grounding: Shows a reviewer who gives specific, timely, kind feedback with a named strength, one concrete spot and a reason.

subtopic: Debugging and problem solving under pressure
passage: Liam stared at the equation on the kitchen table in Leeds, ten minutes before his older sister Olga would check his homework. He changed a plus to a minus. Wrong. He swapped two numbers, divided everything by two, erased the second line and started over. Suddenly the answer matched the one at the back of the book. He grinned, then looked at the page and realised he had no idea which change had done it. Olga glanced over. "Nice. How did you get it?" Liam opened his mouth and closed it. "I just changed stuff until it worked," he said. The next problem looked exactly as impossible as the first.

qa.q: What did Liam change first when he began?
qa.a: Liam changed a plus to a minus.

qa.q: What was Liam feeling when Olga asked how he got the answer?
qa.a: Liam felt caught out and unsure, because he opened his mouth and closed it, knowing he could not say which change had worked.

qa.q: What could Liam do differently on the next problem?
qa.a: He could change one thing at a time and write down what each change did, so he can say why an answer works.

qa.q: How might Olga see Liam's matching answer?
qa.a: Olga may be pleased at first, then notice that a correct answer alone does not show understanding, which is why she asks how he got it.

grounding: Shows a teenager changing things at random on a maths problem and being unable to say what worked.

subtopic: Debugging and problem solving under pressure
passage: In the school computer lab, Gurleen's program printed nothing. She deleted a bracket, retyped a line, renamed a variable and changed 10 to 100. Still nothing. The bell for the end of lab was minutes away and her hands were fast and sweaty. She commented out half the code, brought it back, then pasted a line from the next screen. Numbers suddenly scrolled down. Arnab sir came by. "What fixed it?" Gurleen stared at the screen. "I don't know, sir. Maybe the bracket?" She could not say. He asked her to undo the changes and look at the first error message she had scrolled past. She read it slowly, for the first time.

qa.q: What did Gurleen change 10 to?
qa.a: Gurleen changed 10 to 100.

qa.q: What might Gurleen be worried about as the bell gets closer?
qa.a: She is worried about running out of time and having nothing working, and the panic makes her hands fast and her changes wild.

qa.q: What could Gurleen try instead of changing things at random?
qa.a: She could read the first error message first, then change one thing at a time and check the result each time.

qa.q: What is it like for Arnab sir to see Gurleen produce numbers she cannot explain?
qa.a: Arnab sir sees the program run but knows nothing has been learned, so he asks what fixed it and guides her back to the error message.

grounding: Shows a teenager making frantic random changes to a bug and being unable to say what fixed it.

subtopic: Debugging and problem solving under pressure
subtype: Blaming the tool or the world [Actor]
passage: Beta, I am Madhav, and I once swore that the compiler in our college lab was broken. My program would not run. I told everyone. For two hours I typed the same lines and grew angrier. My lab partner Parul finally pushed back her chair and asked, "Which file is it actually opening?" I snapped that it was obvious. She said, "Humour me." We checked. I had saved my file in a different folder, and the compiler was faithfully running an old copy. Two hours, and the machine had done nothing wrong. I have wondered ever since what else I stopped checking because I felt so sure.

qa.q: What did Madhav swear about the compiler?
qa.a: Madhav swore that the compiler in the college lab was broken.

qa.q: What was Madhav feeling during the two hours before Parul asked her question?
qa.a: Madhav grew angrier and stubbornly certain that the machine was at fault, which is why Madhav told everyone.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story?
qa.a: Parul asked which file the compiler was actually opening, and checking showed the file was saved in a different folder while an old copy ran.

qa.q: Why might Parul have said "Humour me" when Madhav snapped?
qa.a: Parul probably saw that Madhav was too irritated to think and wanted a small check that would test the assumption behind the anger.

grounding: Shows a student blaming the compiler for hours before checking an unverified assumption about which file was running.

subtopic: Debugging and problem solving under pressure
subtype: Blaming the tool or the world [Actor]
passage: With twenty minutes left before the lab submission closed, Swati shoved her laptop across to Saurabh. "The question is wrong. My answer is ten times bigger than the key." Saurabh scrolled up and read for a moment. "Read the first line to me again." She read it out, impatient: "A resistor of four hundred and seventy ohms..." and stopped. Her notes said 4700. She had copied it wrong at the start and built everything on that. She covered her mouth, then fixed the number and reran her working. It matched the key. She pressed submit with two minutes to spare and did not say a word about the question.

qa.q: How many minutes were left before the lab submission closed?
qa.a: Twenty minutes were left before the lab submission closed.

qa.q: What was Swati feeling when she stopped reading the first line aloud?
qa.a: Swati felt startled and a little embarrassed when she saw that the mistake was in her own notes, which is why she covered her mouth.

qa.q: What would you advise Swati to do next time an answer looks wrong?
qa.a: Check the numbers she copied and the steps she assumed before deciding that the question or the key is at fault.

qa.q: How does Saurabh help Swati without making her feel silly?
qa.a: Saurabh just asks her to read the first line aloud, letting her spot the error herself.

grounding: Shows a student insisting the question is wrong before checking her own copied number, an unverified assumption.

subtopic: Debugging and problem solving under pressure
passage: It was one in the morning and my app kept crashing, but only sometimes. Pranav, you had gone to bed, so here is what I did, now that I have finally slept. First I made it crash on purpose, until I saw it happened only when the name field was empty. That was my repeatable case. Second, I cut everything except that one screen. It still crashed. Third, I changed one thing: I gave the field a default. No crash. I wrote each step in my notes: "empty name, crash; default set, fine." Without that list I would have gone in circles, tired as I was. In the morning I read my own list and fixed the check properly. Sunaina

qa.q: When did the app crash?
qa.a: The app crashed only when the name field was empty.

qa.q: How does Sunaina feel about writing each step in the notes?
qa.a: Sunaina feels relieved and grateful to the list, because being tired at one in the morning would have meant going in circles without it.

qa.q: What made the problem easier for Sunaina to solve?
qa.a: Making the crash repeatable, cutting the app down to one screen and changing one thing at a time while writing each result in notes.

qa.q: What might Pranav think of the story if Pranav had been awake and offering many suggestions?
qa.a: Pranav might have offered several guesses at once, which would have made it harder to tell which change made the difference.

grounding: Shows a problem solver making a fault repeatable, isolating it, changing one thing at a time and noting each result.

subtopic: Debugging and problem solving under pressure
passage: At two in the morning the light was still on under Uma's door in the hostel. The study group's marks sheet showed a total that was forty out. I, Lakshmi, sat on the spare chair with my tea and watched. Uma did not shout at the screen. She copied the sheet, made the wrong total appear again in the copy, then deleted columns until the total came right: column D. Then she changed one cell at a time and wrote each result on a scrap of paper: "D7 is text, not a number." I could not tell if she was pleased or too tired to care. She fixed D7, the total matched, and she stuck the scrap above her desk.

qa.q: What was wrong with the study group's marks sheet?
qa.a: The sheet showed a total that was forty out.

qa.q: How can you tell that Uma is patient, and what is uncertain about her mood?
qa.a: She works step by step without shouting, but the narrator could not tell if she was pleased or too tired to care.

qa.q: What would you advise Uma to do if the fault comes back on another sheet?
qa.a: She can follow the same list on a copy: make the wrong total appear again, narrow it down, change one cell at a time and note each result.

qa.q: What is it like for Lakshmi watching Uma work at two in the morning?
qa.a: Lakshmi sits quietly with tea and is curious, but cannot tell what Uma feels inside, only what her careful steps show.

grounding: Shows a problem solver reproducing a fault on a copy, isolating a column, changing one cell at a time and writing down each result.

subtopic: Debugging and problem solving under pressure
passage: Zeenat had stared at the same red error for fifty minutes in the hostel computer room in Nagpur. Her eyes burned; every line looked correct. "I'm going for a walk," she told the screen, and left. Jagdish uncle, the watchman, waved from his stool as she circled the block once and stopped at the tea stall for a biscuit. She thought about nothing in particular, watching a stray dog nap under a scooter. At the gate on her way back it hit her like a small click: "lenght". She had spelt length wrong in one place. She jogged upstairs, fixed it and reran. Green. Jagdish uncle looked up. "Solved?" Zeenat laughed. "Just needed a walk."

qa.q: Where did Zeenat stare at the red error?
qa.a: Zeenat stared at the red error in the hostel computer room in Nagpur.

qa.q: What was Zeenat feeling when she told the screen she was going for a walk?
qa.a: Zeenat felt tired and stuck, since her eyes burned and every line looked correct, but she chose to step away.

qa.q: What made the walk useful for Zeenat?
qa.a: Stepping away let her mind rest, and at the gate she suddenly saw that "length" was spelt wrong in one place.

qa.q: How might Jagdish uncle see Zeenat leaving the computer to walk?
qa.a: Jagdish uncle sees her go past and come back, and his question "Solved?" suggests he sees the walk as a normal way to get unstuck.

grounding: Shows a stuck student stepping away for a short walk and seeing the error at once on return.

subtopic: Debugging and problem solving under pressure
passage:
Alka pushed her tray aside in the canteen. "Okay. Can I explain my circuit to you? You know nothing about circuits, which is perfect."
"Go on," said Irfan.
"So there's a battery here. Then the resistor. Then the LED, which should glow, and it doesn't."
"Does it have a front and a back?"
"The flat side goes to the negative. And on mine the flat side goes to... wait." Alka stopped with her spoon in the air. "It's the wrong way round."
"Did I say something?"
"No. You just listened." She grabbed her bag. "Thank you, Irfan."
"Anytime. Was it that easy?"
"It's always that easy after you say it out loud."

qa.a: Alka wanted to explain her circuit to Irfan, who knows nothing about circuits.

qa.q: What was Alka feeling in the moment she stopped with her spoon in the air?
qa.a: Alka felt sudden surprise and relief on spotting the LED the wrong way round, and it shows in how she grabbed her bag.

qa.q: What did Alka do that made her see the fault?
qa.a: She explained the circuit aloud, step by step, to someone who knew nothing about circuits.

qa.q: How might Irfan feel when Alka thanks Irfan for just listening?
qa.a: Irfan may feel surprised and pleased, since Irfan asked "Did I say something?" and did not know the listening was the help.

subtopic: Debugging and problem solving under pressure
passage:
Thursday. The checkout page on the site Gurleen looked after went down at ten past four, and five people crowded behind her chair. Her heart hammered. She changed three settings at once, then a fourth, and the page still failed. Harsha, the team lead, said quietly, "What changed last?" She stopped typing.
Friday. She wrote a card, "What changed last? One change. Note it. Check." and taped it to her monitor.
The next Wednesday a smaller alert fired. Gurleen breathed out, rolled back the last update, watched the page come back and wrote down the time.

qa.a: The checkout page went down at ten past four on Thursday.

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling as she changed the settings with five people behind her?

qa.a: Harsha sees the pressure and asks a quiet question, "What changed last?", to slow things down.

subtopic: Debugging and problem solving under pressure
passage: I am Minakshi, and my first live failure taught me more than any course. The report job emailed itself twice to every customer, and my whole team stood behind my chair. My hands were cold and my head felt narrow as a tube. In one minute I changed the schedule, then the file path, then restarted the server, and made it worse. Ishita, the senior, sat beside me and said, "Stop. What did it do first?" She wrote on paper: ran, ran again, stopped. One change, then look. It took forty minutes and I hated every one. It taught me to write before I touch.

qa.q: What did the report job do to every customer?
qa.a: The report job emailed itself twice to every customer.

qa.q: What was Minakshi feeling with the team standing behind the chair?
qa.a: Minakshi felt frightened and tunnel-visioned, with cold hands and a head that felt narrow, and rushed several changes.

qa.q: What choice did Ishita make that changed the situation?
qa.a: Ishita told Minakshi to stop and wrote down what the job did in order, which slowed things to one change and a look.

qa.q: How might Ishita have seen Minakshi's rushed changes?
qa.a: Ishita probably saw a frightened junior making things worse, and calmly used a written list instead of adding more guesses.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling a first live failure with a racing heart, several rushed changes and a written one-change method.

subtopic: Debugging and problem solving under pressure

subtopic: Debugging and problem solving under pressure
passage: At the dairy collection centre in the small town, the chiller had stopped at five and the milk kept arriving. Six men shouted theories: the compressor, the wiring, somebody's bad luck. Nilesh, who worked the weighing scale, watched Pallavi, the young secretary, ignore all of it. "Is the power on at the board?" she asked. Yes. "Did the panel light go out or stay on?" Someone checked: stayed on. "Has anything been moved today?" A cleaner admitted pushing a box against the wall. Behind the box, a plug sat half out. Pallavi pushed it in. The hum returned. She wrote the time in the register. Nilesh wondered whether she had guessed it or simply worked down a list.

qa.q: What time did the chiller stop?
qa.a: The chiller stopped at five.

qa.q: What does Nilesh feel while watching Pallavi ignore the men's theories?
qa.a: Nilesh feels curious and impressed, and wonders whether she had guessed the answer or worked down a list.

qa.a: They could check that plugs stay in when boxes are moved and keep a simple list of things to check, like power and the panel light.

qa.a: Pallavi seems calm and focused, since she ignores the noise and works down her questions, though the passage does not say what she feels inside.

subtopic: Debugging and problem solving under pressure
passage: Let me tell you about a bad Thursday, beta. I am Nazia. Our order server had stopped, and I was tracing the fault when my manager Chetan messaged for an update. Ten minutes later, he called. Then he came to my desk, and two directors emailed. Every time I answered, I lost my place in the logs and had to start reading again. Forty minutes went by with nothing fixed. Finally I said to Chetan, "Give me one channel, and I will write there every thirty minutes." He hesitated, then agreed and told the directors. I fixed the fault in the next half hour of quiet.

qa.q: How often did Nazia promise to write updates?
qa.a: Nazia promised to write an update every thirty minutes.

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling as the messages, calls and emails kept coming?
qa.a: Nazia felt pressured and scattered, because each interruption made the place in the logs slip away.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Nazia's story?
qa.a: Nazia asked Chetan for one channel and a set interval for updates, and quiet time let her fix the fault.

qa.q: Why might Chetan have hesitated before agreeing?
qa.a: Chetan probably worried about being left without news while the directors kept asking, which is why he hesitated before agreeing and told them himself.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling being interrupted repeatedly during a fault repair and protecting focus with one channel and a set interval.

subtopic: Debugging and problem solving under pressure
passage: It was the first day of the festival sale, the label printer in the packing room had jammed, and parcels were piling on the belt. Urmila switched the printer off at the wall and knelt beside it while Vaibhav, the floor manager, stood behind her asking every two minutes, "Is it fixed?" Two other staff asked too. Each question made her lose the thread of the paper path she was following. After the fourth, she stood up. "Vaibhav, please ask me only at the top of each quarter hour, and send the others to ask you." He blinked, then nodded and wrote the times on the whiteboard. She knelt again, found a crumpled label edge behind the roller, and the printer whirred back to life.

qa.q: What did Urmila do before she knelt beside the printer?
qa.a: Urmila switched the printer off at the wall.

qa.q: How does Urmila feel as the questions keep coming, and how does it show?
qa.a: Urmila feels interrupted and strained, since each question made her lose the thread of the paper path she was following.

qa.q: What worked in this scene, and why?
qa.a: Urmila asked for updates only at the top of each quarter hour, which protected her focus and still let Vaibhav know what was happening.

qa.q: What might Vaibhav have been worrying about when asking so often?
qa.a: Vaibhav was probably anxious about the parcels piling on the belt on the first day of the sale.

subtopic: Decision-making with incomplete information
passage: Sofia had until the last day of March to choose between the science track and the arts track at her school in Lisbon. In October she said she would wait for a sign. In December she was still waiting. In February her friend Jin signed up for the arts choir, and the science club's summer lab filled up. Sofia lay awake with a tight stomach, checking her phone for someone to decide for her. Two weeks before the deadline she wrote two columns on paper: what she knew, and what she could not know. There was still no sign, and there were fewer choices than in October. She chose science and told her mother.

qa.q: When was the deadline for choosing a track?
qa.a: The deadline was the last day of March.

qa.q: What was Sofia feeling as she lay awake in February?
qa.a: Sofia felt anxious, with a tight stomach, hoping that someone or something would decide for her.

qa.q: What did Sofia do at the two-week mark that helped?
qa.a: She wrote two columns, what she knew and what she could not know, then made a choice and told her mother.

qa.q: How might Jin see Sofia's waiting?
qa.a: Jin, who had already signed up for the choir, might see waiting as safe, without noticing that places were filling up around Sofia.

subtopic: Decision-making with incomplete information
passage: Charu kept the Class 10 stream form in her bag for three weeks. Every day she told herself she would fill it in when she felt sure. On the last Monday it was still blank, and Vandana ma'am, the school counsellor, called her in. "Not sure yet," Charu said, picking at her nails. The commerce batch was already full and only two seats remained in science, but the form needed one choice by evening. "I'm scared of picking wrong," she said. Vandana ma'am asked what Charu had learned about each stream so far. Charu counted on her fingers and was surprised that the list was longer than she thought. She ticked a box before the bell.

qa.q: How long did Charu keep the form in her bag?
qa.a: Charu kept the form in her bag for three weeks.

qa.q: Why did Charu pick at her nails when she said "Not sure yet"?
qa.a: Charu was nervous and afraid of picking wrong, and waiting to feel sure had not made the fear go away.

qa.q: What small step helped Charu move from waiting to choosing?
qa.a: She counted what she had learned about each stream and saw the list was longer than she thought, then ticked a box.

qa.q: How does Vandana ma'am see Charu's blank form?
qa.a: Vandana ma'am sees a student who is scared, and asks what Charu already knows instead of telling her what to choose.

grounding: Shows a teenager waiting for certainty about a stream while choices shrink and worry grows.
